title: David's Wars and His Officials
overview: This chapter lists David's victories over neighboring peoples, notes that their wealth was set aside for a future temple, and ends with the names of his chief officials.

parts.label: Philistines and Moab (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: The Philistines had fought Israel for generations, and David now took their city of Gath. Moab was forced to pay tribute, regular payments showing it was under David's rule, and the parallel account in 2 Samuel 8 adds that he executed many Moabite captives.

parts.label: Defeating Hadadezer (vv. 3-4)
parts.note: Hadadezer ruled Zobah, a strong Aramean (Syrian) kingdom north of Damascus, and it is unclear whether he or David was the one pushing toward the Euphrates River. Hamstringing meant cutting the horses' leg tendons so they could never pull war chariots again, and some numbers here differ from 2 Samuel 8, probably through copying errors.

parts.label: Damascus brought under control (vv. 5-6)
parts.note: Arameans from Damascus came to help Hadadezer and were also defeated, so David stationed troops in their land and made them pay tribute. The writer credits these wins to the LORD, a claim repeated again in verse 13.

parts.label: Treasure set aside (vv. 7-11)
parts.note: Gold shields and large amounts of bronze came to Jerusalem, and Solomon later used the bronze for the temple's great water basin, called the Sea, and its pillars. Tou, king of Hamath and an old enemy of Hadadezer, sent gifts to win David's friendship, and David set all of it apart for the LORD's future house.

parts.label: Victory over Edom (vv. 12-13)
parts.note: Abishai, brother of David's army commander Joab, killed eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt, probably near the Dead Sea. Israel then placed troops in Edom and ruled it.

parts.label: David's government (vv. 14-17)
parts.note: David is described as ruling fairly for all his people, with officials over the army, the royal records, worship and official writing. The Kerethites and Pelethites were his bodyguard of foreign soldiers, and Christians later read this picture of a just king as pointing ahead to Jesus.

think: When a nation's success is credited to God, how do you weigh that claim against what it cost the people on the losing side?
